blindSummary:
This state/province stands out on two counts: customary-leadership authority is at its most institutionalised here, and township queerphobia is the most directly documented. A 2024 university criminology master's thesis explores queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in a township north of the country's main coastal city, situating it within endemic-violence patterns - evidence that the constitutional equality guarantee does not reach daily life here. In addition, the senior traditional monarch of the country's largest ethnic community made public anti-gay statements at a 2012 annual royal ceremony; when a provincial LGBT+ network sought an apology, the national association of traditional leaders defended the monarch and condemned "the gays" for seeking fame - royal and chiefly authority aligning against queer people in this specific jurisdiction.

This jurisdiction also sits in the former segregated-homeland geography where traditional courts adjudicate morality-adjacent matters under customary law with a consent presumption running against the individual: an international human-rights organisation's 2012 analysis warned that a then-pending traditional-courts bill would do exactly that, and a 2019 successor statute was declared unconstitutional on 30 May 2023, with the declaration suspended and the statute's validity extended to give the legislature time to act. No state/province has religious criminal law, and no trans-specific arrest or court-blocked statute applies to a visitor here.

Relative to the two other jurisdictions of the same customary-court type, this one carries the additional weight of an actual field study of queerphobic violence and the royal/traditional-leaders episode, while those two show the jurisdictional risk without a retrieved provincial incident series; the coastal jurisdiction with a functioning metro NGO and state-institution belt marks the other end of the national range. The dossier's under-reporting caveat means the absence of a trans-specific incident register here is not exculpatory.
blindSourceSummaries: A 2024 master's thesis in the provincial university's criminology programme: a field-researched exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in a township north of the country's main coastal city - documenting violence against queer people despite the constitutional equality guarantee, within the country's pervasive crime and hate-crime context.

An LGBT-news-outlet report (26 January 2012) on the fallout from the senior traditional monarch's anti-gay remarks at an annual harvest ceremony: the royal family called the reported 'rotten' wording a mistranslation, the national human-rights commission said it would investigate, the provincial premier backed the royal family, and the national association of traditional leaders said the provincial LGBT+ network that demanded an apology had shown the monarch 'disrespect' and were 'only seeking fame'.

An international human-rights organisation's news analysis (29 May 2012): warns that a then-pending traditional-courts bill, giving chiefs sole legal authority, would set up a separate legal system for people living in the former homeland territories and undermine the protections of the bill of rights, with particular consequences for gender and sexual rights.
blindOutOfScope: Interpersonal violent crime in townships is high for all travellers, and the 2024 field study itself frames queerphobic violence within that endemic-violence context; the finding relevant to this jurisdiction is the targeting pattern and the royal/chiefly climate, not the baseline crime rate.
blindTangential: The royal and traditional-leaders' hostility documented here is voiced against 'the gays' - sexual orientation rather than gender identity - but it sets an official chiefly climate in which any queer visibility, including trans presence, is publicly repudiated by the jurisdiction's most senior traditional institutions.
